name: Harold Holt
bio: One of the young men of George Ives's household; Cook identifies him as Ives's grandmother's former secretary, named alongside James Goddard as sharing Ives's rooms at E4 the Albany - and sometimes his bed - from 1894.
bio_sources: Cook, London and the Culture of Homosexuality (2003), pp. 146, 148
bio_note: SOURCE CONFLICT - UNRESOLVED, needs human adjudication. Cook 2003 p. 146 (read in the source 2026-08-03) names the two men sharing Ives's bed as 'James Goddard (Kit)' and 'Harold Holt (Cubby)'. Cook 2014 p. 101 (repo PDF 112, folio confirmed, read in the source 2026-08-03) instead identifies the long-term resident nicknamed Cubby as 'Charles Gee'. The same author gives two different men behind the same nickname eleven years apart. Possibilities: a correction in the later book; two successive residents sharing a nickname; or an error in one text. This record is retained under the Cook 2003 name pending adjudication - do NOT merge, rename, or create a 'Charles Gee' node until Lovelle decides. Original note: Facts from Cook, London and the Culture of Homosexuality (2003), p. 146, read as a page image 2026-08-03 by the Ives research pass (repo PDF 162; printed folio confirmed). Birth and death dates not established in the works read. Promoted from an ives.json context engagement to a roster node 2026-08-03. DATES: NOT FOUND; RECORDED AS UNRECOVERED (2026-08-03), and note that the source position is weaker for him than for the rest of the household. Harold Holt does not appear in Cook 2014 at all - a search of the whole repo PDF returns no occurrence of the name - so the only source for him remains Cook 2003 p. 146, which names him but gives no dates, and Cook 2014 assigns the nickname Cubby to a different man (Charles Gee), the unresolved conflict already recorded above. Until that conflict is adjudicated, date research on 'Harold Holt' risks being research on the wrong person. Searched so far, WITHOUT RESULT: Cook, Queer Domesticities (2014), repo PDF - every occurrence of the surname in the whole book, plus the endnotes and bibliography for the household chapter; the Ives repo transcripts (ives_diaries_burnet.txt, ives_letters_burnet_collated.txt, ives_letters_burnet_transcription.txt, ives_lewis_correspondence_2026-06.md), which contain no occurrence of any of the household surnames; and the open web, which returned only the Palgrave chapter version of Cook's same text ('George Ives, Queer Lives and the Family') and no dates. Cook is the only scholar to have written this household up and he dates their arrivals, their departures and Ives's will, but never a person: he gives no birth or death date for any member of the household. WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY CLOSE IT: census, GRO index and probate research on common English surnames - work so far could not do. Ives's own proved will (Cook, printed pp. 109-110), which leaves the Adelaide Road house to Bloodworth and Saunders, names Bloodworth an executor and portions the Goddards, is the natural documentary starting point, since a grant of probate fixes addresses and often identifies legatees.
